items.stem: What is the key feature of the Von Neumann architecture?
options: Each instruction has its own processor
Instructions and data are stored in separate memories
Instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory
items.answer: Instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory
items.markingKey: Stored-program concept: program and data share memory and buses; one instruction fetched at a time.

items.stem: Explain the difference between general-purpose registers and special-purpose registers.
items.answer: General-purpose registers (e.g. ACC) hold any data being processed; special-purpose registers (e.g. PC, MAR, MDR, CIR) each have one specific role in the fetch–execute cycle.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: general purpose — temporary data/any use; 1 mark: special purpose — dedicated function with example [2]

items.stem: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional but the data bus is bidirectional.
items.answer: Only the processor sends addresses to memory/devices; data must travel both from memory to the processor (read) and from the processor to memory (write).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: address only from CPU; 1 mark: data both ways (read and write) [2]

items.stem: A student at BlueWave Supermarkets is using a simulator to watch the registers of a Von Neumann processor. Identify the bus used to send the address of an instruction to memory and the bus used to return the instruction.
items.answer: Address bus; data bus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student at Starlight Cinemas is using a simulator to watch the registers of a Von Neumann processor. (a) Identify the bus used to send the address of an instruction to memory and the bus used to return the instruction. (b) The address bus has 20 lines. Calculate how many memory locations can be addressed.
items.answer: (a) Address bus; data bus. (b) 1,048,576

items.stem: The processor in a laptop used by Isla is executing a program stored in RAM. (a) Describe the role of the control unit during the execution of an ADD instruction. (b) Explain why the processor has a clock. (c) The address bus has 12 lines. Calculate how many memory locations can be addressed.
items.answer: (a) Decodes the instruction and sends control signals so the operand is fetched and the ALU adds it to the ACC. (b) To synchronise operations; each step occurs on a clock pulse. (c) 4,096
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark decode; 1 mark control signals to ALU/registers [2] (b) 1 mark [1] (c) 2^12 = 4,096 [1]

items.stem: Summit Engineering is designing a simple processor for an embedded controller, based on the Von Neumann model. (a) Describe the roles of the PC, MAR and CIR when an instruction is fetched. (b) State the purpose of the IX register.
items.answer: (a) PC holds address of next instruction, copied to MAR; instruction copied (via MDR) into CIR for decoding; PC incremented. (b) Holds a value added to an address for indexed addressing (e.g. stepping through an array).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per register role [3] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Tomás is writing a revision guide explaining how a Von Neumann processor works. (a) Describe the roles of the PC, MAR and CIR when an instruction is fetched. (b) Explain the purpose of the status register.
items.answer: (a) PC holds address of next instruction, copied to MAR; instruction copied (via MDR) into CIR for decoding; PC incremented. (b) Its flags record the outcome of operations (zero, negative, carry, overflow), used by conditional instructions and interrupt handling.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per register role [3] (b) 1 mark: flags; 1 mark: use [2]

items.stem: Which bus is unidirectional?
items.answer: Address bus
items.markingKey: Address bus: CPU → memory only; data and control buses are bidirectional.

items.stem: What is the role of the control unit (CU)?
options: To perform arithmetic and logic operations
To decode instructions and send control signals to coordinate the other components
To store the next instruction address
items.answer: To decode instructions and send control signals to coordinate the other components
items.markingKey: CU: decodes, sends signals on the control bus, synchronises with clock.

items.stem: Explain the role of the status register after a subtraction gives a negative result.
items.answer: The negative flag is set to 1 (and possibly carry/overflow flags), so a later conditional jump can test it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: flag set; 1 mark: used by conditional instructions [2]

items.stem: Describe the role of the MAR and MDR when data is read from memory.
items.answer: The address is placed in the MAR and sent on the address bus; the data at that address is sent on the data bus into the MDR.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MAR holds address; 1 mark: MDR receives data [2]

items.stem: A student at Atlas Museum is using a simulator to watch the registers of a Von Neumann processor. State the full name of the PC register and describe its role.
items.answer: Program Counter: holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched
items.markingKey: 1 mark name; 1 mark role [2]

items.stem: A student at Lakeside College is using a simulator to watch the registers of a Von Neumann processor. (a) State the full name of the ACC register and describe its role. (b) The address bus has 24 lines. Calculate how many memory locations can be addressed.
items.answer: (a) Accumulator: a general-purpose register that holds values being processed and the results of ALU operations (b) 16,777,216

items.stem: Diego is writing a revision guide explaining how a Von Neumann processor works. (a) Describe the roles of the PC, MAR and CIR when an instruction is fetched. (b) Explain the Von Neumann bottleneck and one way to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) PC holds address of next instruction, copied to MAR; instruction copied (via MDR) into CIR for decoding; PC incremented. (b) Data and instructions share one bus so cannot be fetched at once, limiting speed; reduce with cache memory or separate buses/Harvard design.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per register role [3] (b) 1 mark: shared bus; 1 mark: limits speed; 1 mark: cache/separate buses [3]

items.stem: What is meant by clock speed?
options: The time taken to boot the computer
The width of the data bus
The number of programs run per second
The number of clock cycles the processor completes per second
items.answer: The number of clock cycles the processor completes per second
items.markingKey: Measured in Hz (e.g. 3.2 GHz = 3.2 × 10⁹ cycles per second).

items.stem: Explain how cache memory improves the performance of a processor.
items.answer: Frequently used data/instructions are stored in fast cache near the CPU, so they are fetched more quickly than from RAM, reducing the time the processor waits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: stores frequently used data/instructions; 1 mark: faster access than RAM; 1 mark: less waiting / fewer RAM fetches [3]

items.stem: Explain why increasing clock speed can cause problems.
items.answer: More heat is generated, which may cause instability or damage, so better cooling is needed; components may not keep up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: heat; 1 mark: consequence [2]

items.stem: A 1 GHz processor takes an average of 4 clock cycles to execute each instruction. Calculate the number of instructions executed per second.
items.answer: 250 million
items.markingKey: 1 × 10⁹ cycles per second ÷ 4 = 250 × 10⁶ instructions per second [2]

items.stem: Data is transferred across a 32-bit data bus, one transfer per clock cycle. Calculate how many clock cycles are needed to transfer 512 bytes, and state the effect of doubling the bus width.
items.answer: 128 cycles; halved to 64
items.markingKey: 512 × 8 = 4096 bits [1]; ÷ 32 = 128 cycles [1]; doubling width halves cycles to 64 [1] [3]

items.stem: Starlight Cinemas must choose new processors for its servers in Cairo. Option 1: 4 cores at 4.0 GHz, 8 MiB cache. Option 2: 16 cores at 2.6 GHz, 32 MiB cache. (a) Explain how the number of cores affects performance for this use. (b) Describe how a larger cache improves performance.
items.answer: (a) More cores let independent tasks/threads run at once; video editing/servers have many parallel tasks so benefit. (b) More frequently used data/instructions fit in fast cache, fewer slow RAM accesses.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: parallel execution; 1 mark: linked to the use [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how a multi-core processor can improve performance.
items.answer: Each core can fetch and execute instructions independently, so different tasks/threads run at the same time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cores execute independently; 1 mark: parallel tasks [2]

(a) Explain why the option with the lower clock speed may still perform better. (b) Give one factor, other than the processor, that affects the computer's performance.
items.answer: (a) More cores and larger cache can outweigh lower clock speed when tasks are parallel and data is reused. (b) Amount of RAM, storage speed (SSD), bus width, GPU.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark cores; 1 mark cache; 1 mark conclusion [3] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: In register transfer notation, what does MAR ← [PC] mean?
options: The address in the PC is incremented
The contents of the PC are copied into the MAR
The MAR is copied into the PC
items.answer: The contents of the PC are copied into the MAR
items.markingKey: Square brackets mean "the contents of"; ← means "is copied into".

items.stem: Describe the fetch stage of the fetch–execute cycle using register transfer notation.
items.answer: MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR].
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct step in order [4]

items.stem: Explain why the PC is incremented during the fetch stage.
items.answer: So that it holds the address of the next instruction, ready for the next cycle (unless a jump changes it).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: points to next instruction; 1 mark: ready for next fetch / jump may overwrite [2]

items.stem: In the fetch stage, which register transfer happens immediately after MDR ← [[MAR]]?
items.answer: CIR ← [MDR]
items.markingKey: Order: MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR].

items.markingKey: 1 mark each: PC 110; MAR 109; MDR ADD 824; CIR ADD 824 [4]

items.stem: What is an interrupt?
options: An instruction to delete a program
A fault that permanently stops the computer
A signal to the processor that a device or program needs attention
items.answer: A signal to the processor that a device or program needs attention
items.markingKey: Interrupts can come from hardware (e.g. printer out of paper) or software (e.g. division by zero).

items.stem: Describe the sequence of steps taken by the processor when an interrupt is detected.
items.answer: At end of current cycle, check priority; save registers (PC etc.) on the stack; load PC with start address of the ISR; run ISR; restore registers from the stack; continue original program.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per step in order, max 4 [4]

items.stem: Explain why interrupts are given priorities.
items.answer: Some events (e.g. power failure, hardware fault) are more urgent; a higher-priority interrupt can interrupt a lower-priority ISR, so critical events are handled first.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: some more urgent; 1 mark: higher priority handled first/can interrupt lower [2]

items.stem: A program written by Samuel attempts to divide a number by zero. Explain what happens to the current task when the interrupt is serviced.
items.answer: Its registers are saved on the stack; the ISR runs; registers restored and the task resumes.

items.stem: Noah is printing a long report at Peak Fitness while editing a spreadsheet. (a) Identify the interrupt in this situation and state whether it is a hardware or software interrupt. (b) Explain why the processor checks for interrupts only at the end of a fetch–execute cycle.
items.answer: (a) e.g. printer out of paper/buffer empty (hardware); power failure (hardware); division by zero (software). (b) So that the current instruction completes and the state can be saved consistently.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark interrupt; 1 mark type [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Nadia is writing a report on how operating systems manage hardware. Evaluate the importance of interrupts in a multitasking operating system.
items.answer: Points in favour: devices signal when ready so CPU does not waste time polling; urgent events handled at once; enables time-slicing via timer interrupts. Points against / limitations: too many interrupts add overhead from saving/restoring registers; badly prioritised interrupts can delay important tasks. Conclusion: interrupts are essential for efficient multitasking but need careful priority management.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: devices signal when ready so CPU does not waste time polling; urgent events handled at once; enables time-slicing via timer interrupts. / too many interrupts add overhead from saving/restoring registers; badly prioritised interrupts can delay important tasks. [6]

items.stem: What is the purpose of the system clock?
options: To generate timing signals that synchronise the components of the processor
To show the time to the user
To store the date of files
To count the number of programs running
items.answer: To generate timing signals that synchronise the components of the processor
items.markingKey: Clock pulses: each step of the fetch–execute cycle occurs on a clock tick.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The address bus is unidirectional. Reason (R): The data bus is unidirectional. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is true but R is false
items.markingKey: A is true; R is false: "The data bus is unidirectional." is incorrect.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the address bus is unidirectional but the data bus is bidirectional. (b) Explain the role of the status register after a subtraction gives a negative result.
items.answer: (a) Only the processor sends addresses to memory/devices; data must travel both from memory to the processor (read) and from the processor to memory (write). (b) The negative flag is set to 1 (and possibly carry/overflow flags), so a later conditional jump can test it.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: address only from CPU; 1 mark: data both ways (read and write) [2] (b) 1 mark: flag set; 1 mark: used by conditional instructions [2]

items.stem: A student at Sunrise Bakery is using a simulator to watch the registers of a Von Neumann processor. Describe the role of the control unit during the execution of an ADD instruction.
items.answer: Decodes the instruction and sends control signals so the operand is fetched and the ALU adds it to the ACC.
items.markingKey: 1 mark decode; 1 mark control signals to ALU/registers [2]

items.stem: The processor in a laptop used by Grace is executing a program stored in RAM. (a) Describe the role of the control unit during the execution of an ADD instruction. (b) Explain why the processor has a clock.
items.answer: (a) Decodes the instruction and sends control signals so the operand is fetched and the ALU adds it to the ACC. (b) To synchronise operations; each step occurs on a clock pulse.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark decode; 1 mark control signals to ALU/registers [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Orbit Games Studio is designing a simple processor for an embedded controller, based on the Von Neumann model. (a) Explain the Von Neumann bottleneck and one way to reduce it. (b) Explain the purpose of the status register.
items.answer: (a) Data and instructions share one bus so cannot be fetched at once, limiting speed; reduce with cache memory or separate buses/Harvard design. (b) Its flags record the outcome of operations (zero, negative, carry, overflow), used by conditional instructions and interrupt handling.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: shared bus; 1 mark: limits speed; 1 mark: cache/separate buses [3] (b) 1 mark: flags; 1 mark: use [2]

items.stem: What is the main effect of increasing the width of the address bus?
options: More memory locations can be addressed
items.answer: More memory locations can be addressed
items.markingKey: n address lines → 2ⁿ locations.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how cache memory improves the performance of a processor. (b) Explain how a multi-core processor can improve performance.
items.answer: (a) Frequently used data/instructions are stored in fast cache near the CPU, so they are fetched more quickly than from RAM, reducing the time the processor waits. (b) Each core can fetch and execute instructions independently, so different tasks/threads run at the same time.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: stores frequently used data/instructions; 1 mark: faster access than RAM; 1 mark: less waiting / fewer RAM fetches [3] (b) 1 mark: cores execute independently; 1 mark: parallel tasks [2]

items.stem: Data is transferred across a 16-bit data bus, one transfer per clock cycle. Calculate how many clock cycles are needed to transfer 256 bytes, and state the effect of doubling the bus width.
items.answer: 128 cycles; halved to 64
items.markingKey: 256 × 8 = 2048 bits [1]; ÷ 16 = 128 cycles [1]; doubling width halves cycles to 64 [1] [3]

items.stem: Orbit Games Studio must choose new processors for its servers in Lisbon. Option 1: 4 cores at 4.0 GHz, 8 MiB cache. Option 2: 16 cores at 2.6 GHz, 32 MiB cache. (a) Describe how a larger cache improves performance. (b) Make and justify a recommendation.
items.answer: (a) More frequently used data/instructions fit in fast cache, fewer slow RAM accesses. (b) Choose the multi-core, large-cache option for parallel workloads; the higher clock speed option for single-threaded tasks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark choice; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is a feature of USB? (b) In register transfer notation, what does MAR ← [PC] mean?
items.answer: (a) Devices are automatically detected and can be powered through the cable (b) The contents of the PC are copied into the MAR
items.markingKey: (a) USB: plug and play, standard connector, supplies power, many devices on one controller. (b) Square brackets mean "the contents of"; ← means "is copied into".

items.stem: Ines writes the fetch stage as: CIR ← [MDR]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; MAR ← [PC]. Identify the error and write the correct sequence.
items.answer: Steps "MAR ← [PC]" and "CIR ← [MDR]" are in the wrong order. Correct: MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR].
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the misplaced steps with reason; 1 mark: correct order [2]

items.stem: In the fetch stage, which register transfer happens immediately after MAR ← [PC]?
items.answer: PC ← [PC] + 1
items.markingKey: Order: MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR].

items.stem: In the fetch stage, which register transfer happens immediately after MDR ← [[MAR]]?
items.answer: CIR ← [MDR]
items.markingKey: Order: MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR].

items.stem: The PC contains 185. Memory location 185 contains the instruction LDD 835. Give the contents of the PC, MAR, MDR and CIR at the end of the fetch stage.
items.answer: PC = 186, MAR = 185, MDR = LDD 835, CIR = LDD 835
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: PC 186; MAR 185; MDR LDD 835; CIR LDD 835 [4]

items.stem: A technician at GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Colombo is connecting monitors, printers and an old projector to classroom computers, and is explaining to students how the processor runs programs. (a) Describe the fetch stage using register transfer notation. (b) Explain why USB devices can be connected without restarting the computer.
items.answer: (a) MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR]. (b) USB is plug and play / hot-swappable: the OS detects the device and loads the driver automatically.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per step [4] (b) 1 mark detection; 1 mark driver loaded [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the sequence of steps taken by the processor when an interrupt is detected. (b) Explain the difference between a hardware interrupt and a software interrupt, giving an example of each.
items.answer: (a) At end of current cycle, check priority; save registers (PC etc.) on the stack; load PC with start address of the ISR; run ISR; restore registers from the stack; continue original program. (b) Hardware: generated by a device (printer out of paper, key press); software: generated by a program (division by zero, request for OS service).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per step in order, max 4 [4] (b) 1 mark each with example [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe the sequence of steps taken by the processor when an interrupt is detected. (b) Explain the difference between a hardware interrupt and a software interrupt, giving an example of each.
items.answer: (a) At end of current cycle, check priority; save registers (PC etc.) on the stack; load PC with start address of the ISR; run ISR; restore registers from the stack; continue original program. (b) Hardware: generated by a device (printer out of paper, key press); software: generated by a program (division by zero, request for OS service).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per step in order, max 4 [4] (b) 1 mark each with example [2]

items.stem: Mateo is printing a long report at MetroBus while editing a spreadsheet. Identify the interrupt in this situation and state whether it is a hardware or software interrupt.
items.answer: e.g. printer out of paper/buffer empty (hardware); power failure (hardware); division by zero (software).
items.markingKey: 1 mark interrupt; 1 mark type [2]

items.stem: City Central Library in Kuala Lumpur runs many programs at the same time on each computer. Discuss the importance of interrupts in a multitasking operating system.
items.answer: Points in favour: devices signal when ready so CPU does not waste time polling; urgent events handled at once; enables time-slicing via timer interrupts. Points against / limitations: too many interrupts add overhead from saving/restoring registers; badly prioritised interrupts can delay important tasks. Conclusion: interrupts are essential for efficient multitasking but need careful priority management.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: devices signal when ready so CPU does not waste time polling; urgent events handled at once; enables time-slicing via timer interrupts. / too many interrupts add overhead from saving/restoring registers; badly prioritised interrupts can delay important tasks.
